## Motivation

The argument that the C-section trajectory is not a single phenomenon — that it is a *regime transition* with two qualitatively different selection mechanisms before and after roughly 2011 — needs descriptive evidence. Sector decomposition is the strongest single piece: within the public sector, the C-section rate stayed roughly constant from 2004 to 2022; within the private sector, it nearly doubled, *and* the private sector grew to over four-fifths of all C-section deliveries [@sujon2025cesarean].

This is precisely the kind of structural change that breaks IV identification: not the level shifts, but the change in *what the instrument means* over time [@angrist2014peer; @betz2018spatial].

## Data and setup

Sector decomposition data come from `data/processed/descriptive/P1_Sector_Decomp_All.csv`. Each row is a country × year × sector combination with two values: the within-sector C-section rate, and the sector's share of total C-section deliveries.

#| echo: false

## Interpretation

The decomposition is unambiguous: the rise in the national C-section rate is overwhelmingly a private-sector phenomenon. Public-sector C-section rates are nearly flat over eighteen years.

That fact alone changes how the instrument should be read in Part II. The "community-level leave-one-out C-section rate" — the instrument used by the RBVP in Chapter 7 — captures different things in different waves:

- In 2004, a high community C-section rate signals proximity to a working obstetric facility (supply-side geography).
- In 2022, a high community C-section rate signals private-sector density, social norms, provider-induced demand (demand-side selection).

The exclusion restriction — that the IV affects mortality *only* through individual C-section status — is implausible in *either* regime, but for different reasons. Chapter 6 lays out the framework; Chapter 9 runs the cross-instrument placebo that decisively rejects the assumption.
